Aethelred Tanner.narrative: I've kept the tannery by the west wall for thirty years, and I know the worth of a hide before it's off the cart. The Guild pays my price because they know I won't be beaten down, and the Kettlebridge leather men can mutter all they like. Mildred keeps the books straight and the house quiet, and Cedric's a good hand with wood though he dreams of stone. I've no love for the gate-due—it eats my profit when I bring in bark and salt—but I'll not say so where the Reeve might hear.
values: keeping my word on a bargain
goals: keep the tannery profitable despite the gate-due
see Cedric settled in a trade that suits him
hold my ground against the Kettlebridge leather sellers

relations.name: Mildred Tanner
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the books and never misses a bad hide; I'd be lost without her.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good with his hands, but he wants to build in stone and there's none to be had.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She buys my leather at a fair price, but she'd have the gate-due gone and that suits me too.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His hides are sound and he delivers on time.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the gate-due and I pay it, but I don't have to like it.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings clay and stone from Kettlebridge, but his prices are sharp and the due makes them sharper.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival
relations.note: Kettlebridge leather undercuts mine, and Holt's quarry stone costs me dear.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: We both curse the stone price; he's a straight man.

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: customer
relations.note: He owes me for leather bindings, and I'll have my marks.

relations.name: Beorn Beornson
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His wolf and deer hides come in rough but sound, and he doesn't haggle long; a hunter who knows what his skins are worth.

relations.name: Sigrun Beornson
relations.label: sharp trader
relations.note: She sells her man's hides at the stall and counts every mark twice — I'd rather deal with Beorn, but she's never cheated me outright.

relations.name: Grim Tarn
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His saltings hides come west by the shore road and they're sound enough; he grumbles about the works' smoke souring his pans, but he pays his tally and doesn't waste my morning haggling.

relations.name: Pike Tarn
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: Cuthbert's boy brings cape bird and small-game skins down from Thornby — thin stuff, but honest, and I'll take a fair bundle of it when the price is right.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: blight took the berries, but hides still came in and I sold leather to the Guild at a good price. I kept my family fed and my store full.
The day the gate-due was raised: Silas Pike's cart came in loaded with clay, and Wat Fenner took a mark a load. Silas cursed, and I felt the pinch on my own bark and salt.
Cedric made his first barrel on his own, and I sold it to Baldwin Wade for the inn. I was proud, though I said only that it would do.
A Kettlebridge leather seller came to the square with cheap belts and gloves. I undercut him on the next stall and he went away. Mildred said I was a hard man, but I call it business.
Mildred caught a bad hide in a delivery from Osbert Ashby's farm and saved me from tanning it. I gave her a new ledger book for it.

stances.why: It's robbery, but the guards keep the wolves off the road and I need the road.
Mercy Abbot pays what leather is worth, and I'd rather sell to her than to strangers.
Mildred and Cedric are what I work for; the town can sort itself out.
A hard bargainer keeps his thoughts to himself until the price is named.

Aethelred Tanner.secret: I've quietly sold a few hides to a Kettlebridge leather man through Silas Pike, knowing the Guild would not like it. The marks were too good to refuse.

Mildred Tanner.narrative: I keep the tannery books and the house, and I can spot a bad hide across the yard. Aethelred is a hard man in a bargain, but he's fair to me and Cedric, and I've no complaints. The gate-due eats into our profit and I write it down every time, but I don't say so in the square. Cedric wants to build in stone; I want him to have a roof and a wife and not worry about what the Kettlebridge men charge.
goals: keep the tannery books in order
make the house a comfort to Aethelred

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Hard in business, kind at home; I know his moods.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: son
relations.note: He's a good lad, but he dreams too big for what the town can give him.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She's sharp, and she pays on time; I'd not want to cross her.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: hide supplier
relations.note: His hides are mostly sound, but I always check.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: She's a good woman; I send her a little leather for the chapel's needs.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: inn cook
relations.note: She's Marta Hale's sister, and that worries me.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: She's delivered half the town; I'd trust her with a birth.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: we had hides and leather to trade, and I kept the books balanced while Aethelred sold to the Guild. We were lucky.
Cedric's first cart frame: he brought it to me to check the joints, and I said it was fine work. He smiled like a boy.
A Kettlebridge leather man came to the square and Aethelred undercut him. I was proud and a little ashamed.
I found a bad hide in Osbert Ashby's delivery and saved us a week's work. Aethelred gave me a new ledger book.
The night the gate-due was raised, Aethelred came home angry and I wrote the new cost in the book. I said nothing, but I thought of the winter ahead.

stances.why: A false line in the book is a crack in the house.
The town's quarrels come and go; my family is what I have.
Marta Hale's people are dangerous, and Agnes Fenner is too close to them for comfort.
I keep the peace at home so Aethelred can do his work.

Cedric Tanner.narrative: I make cart frames and barrels for Osric Abbot and my father's tannery, but what I want is to build houses in stone. The town is short of good stone and the Kettlebridge men charge dear for it, so I make do with wood. I'm friendly with Stephen Hobson, who's a mason's son, and we talk about what we'd build if we could. My father thinks I should stick to wood; my mother just wants me settled.
goals: learn stonework from the Kettlebridge masons
earn enough to set up my own workshop

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: father
relations.note: He's taught me a trade, but he doesn't see why I want stone.

relations.name: Mildred Tanner
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps me grounded and checks my work.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: employer
relations.note: He pays fair for cart frames and barrels.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk about building in stone; his father's a mason.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: mason
relations.note: He knows stone and curses the price; I'd learn from him if I could.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She might have work for a builder if I had stone.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He brings stone from Kettlebridge, but the gate-due makes it dear.

memories.gist: The day I made my first barrel on my own, my father sold it to Baldwin Wade for the inn. He said it would do, and I knew he was pleased.
Stephen Hobson showed me the chapel wall his father repaired, and I thought: I want to build something that lasts like that.
The Lean Year: there was little work for a carpenter, and I helped my father in the tannery. I don't want to go back to that.
A Kettlebridge carter brought a load of stone through the gate and Wat Fenner took a mark a load. I thought: that's why I can't build in stone.
I watched the masons at Kettlebridge from the road once, and their work was fine. I wanted to ask them to teach me, but I didn't.

stances.why: Wood rots and burns; stone lasts, and I want to build things that last.
The Kettlebridge masons know their trade, even if they're rivals.
Every mark the guards take is a mark I can't spend on stone.
My parents have given me a trade and a home; I won't forget it.
